clue.text: A boy is opening beer for tailor

parts.note: a can mean per, 'for each', as in 'ten pounds a head'
a son is a boy child

indicators.note: opening is a verb here: one piece opens up the word for beer and sits inside it

parts.note: ale is a kind of beer
taken as written

explanation.surface: A lad is cracking open a bottle of ale for the man who makes his suits.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface has a lad pouring a tailor a drink, but 'tailor' is a verb and 'A' is PER, as in 'ten pounds a head'. 'opening' makes the little verb 'is' break into the beer.
explanation.definitionFit: Verb synonyms: both mean adapting something to suit one particular individual, as a bank does with its services.

clue.text: Bar university cutting lead

indicators.note: cutting means slicing into, so the university's letter splits the symbol for lead in two

parts.note: Pb is the chemical symbol for the metal lead, from the Latin plumbum

explanation.surface: Ban the university that keeps trimming its advantage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bar' reads as a verb meaning exclude, but it is a noun, and 'lead' is the metal, not an advantage: 'cutting' sets U inside its symbol, PB.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonyms: both are licensed premises where drinks are sold over a counter, the second being the British kind.

clue.text: Former law officer often seen with ruff?

definitions.meaning: in medieval England this was the chief magistrate of a town or district, keeping order for the king; the office died out, hence 'Former'
the ruff is a wading bird, and the female of the species has a name of her own; she is naturally found alongside the male

explanation.surface: A lawman of bygone days, usually pictured wearing a frilly Elizabethan collar.
explanation.walkthrough: The ruff looks like the frilled Elizabethan collar an old official would wear, but it is the wading bird, whose female is called a reeve. The question mark flags that punning second definition.
explanation.definitionFit: An old English magistrate bore this title, and it is also the name of the female of the wading bird called the ruff.

clue.text: No longer in use, my empty old menageries impressing king

indicators.note: empty tells you to remove the contents of the next word, keeping only its first and last letters
impressing is pressing in: the word for menageries has the king's letter pressed into it

parts.note: a menagerie is a collection of captive animals, a zoo; the plural gives the plural
K is the abbreviation for king in chess and cards

explanation.surface: Someone's abandoned old animal collections, though empty and disused, still awe a monarch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'my' is the exclamation of surprise, not a possessive, and 'No longer in use' marks it as archaic. 'empty' leaves OD from old, and 'impressing' presses K into ZOOS.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are exclamations of surprise; this one is an archaic minced oath, a variant of gadzooks, long obsolete.

clue.text: Much travelled bird, one under 21

definitions.meaning: a huge seabird famous for gliding thousands of miles over the southern oceans without touching land
the answer at 21 down is the golf score of two under par on a hole; one stroke lower still, three under par, has this bird's name

explanation.surface: A bird that has seen much of the world despite being not yet twenty-one.
explanation.walkthrough: '21' is not an age but a cross-reference to 21 down, EAGLE. In golf an eagle is two under par on a hole, and an albatross is one stroke better, three under.
explanation.definitionFit: It is both a seabird that roams the southern oceans for years and golf's name for three under par, one better than two under.

clue.text: Inspire revolutionary EU health indicator

indicators.note: revolutionary suggests turning right round, so everything after it is read from the last letter to the first

parts.note: taken as written
BMI, body mass index, is the standard measure of whether your weight is healthy for your height

explanation.surface: Spark the creation of a radical new European measure of public health.
explanation.walkthrough: 'revolutionary' turns the whole run EU plus BMI (body mass index) back to front: EUBMI becomes IMBUE. The radical European policy of the surface is a decoy.
explanation.definitionFit: Near-synonyms as verbs: each means to fill someone with a feeling or quality, such as confidence.

clue.text: Extend green ground outside city

indicators.note: outside says the rearranged letters go around the letters for the city
ground is the past tense of grind, so the word before it is milled into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, as the letters to be milled
LA, Los Angeles, is a city crosswords use constantly

explanation.surface: Make the grassy playing field on the edge of town bigger.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ground' is not a playing field but the past tense of grind, milling the colour into ENRGE. 'outside' then sets those letters around the city, the American one crosswords love.
explanation.definitionFit: Verb synonyms: both mean to make something bigger, as you do when adding rooms to a house.

clue.text: Halfpenny collar?

indicators.note: Half, split off from the front of Halfpenny, keeps only the first three letters of a six-letter word for a penny

parts.note: a copper is British slang for a penny, a small brown coin once made of that metal

explanation.surface: A shirt collar so cheap that it costs only a halfpenny.
explanation.walkthrough: The halfpenny, an old British coin, must be split in two: 'Half' keeps the first three letters of COPPER, British slang for a penny. To collar a suspect is to catch or arrest them.
explanation.definitionFit: Slang synonyms as verbs: both mean to seize or arrest someone, as police do with a suspect.

clue.text: Valets abused in French company? Such is life there

indicators.note: in tells you the mistreated letters sit within the abbreviation for a French firm

parts.note: Cie is the French abbreviation for Compagnie, the equivalent of Co. in a firm's name

indicators.note: abused means treated roughly, so the letters of the word before it are knocked out of order

parts.note: taken as written, as the letters to be knocked about

explanation.surface: Manservants are mistreated at a firm in France, but that is just how things go over there.
explanation.walkthrough: 'abused' rearranges the manservants into ESTLAV, and 'in' drops that into the French for Co. 'there' points back across the Channel, so the definition wants the saying in French, not English.
explanation.definitionFit: Translation: the French say this, literally 'that is life', with a resigned shrug, and 'there' means across the Channel in France.

clue.text: Familiar stars split tiller

parts.note: the Plough is the British name for the Big Dipper, seven bright stars that form one of the best-known shapes in the sky
to split a bill or a prize is to share it

explanation.surface: Well-known celebrities broke the boat's steering handle in two.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tiller' reads as a boat's steering handle, but here it is a thing that tills the soil. The Plough is the British name for the Big Dipper, seven of the sky's best-known stars.
explanation.definitionFit: Literal agent noun: it is the blade that cuts the furrow, so it is a thing that tills the soil.

clue.text: Old nick's auntie harnessing large ox

indicators.note: to harness an animal is to strap it in, so auntie's letters hold the other pieces inside them

parts.note: Auntie is the affectionate British nickname for the BBC, which is also known as the Beeb
L is the clothing-label abbreviation for large
a zebu is the humped ox of South Asia

explanation.surface: The Devil's aunt is strapping a big ox into its harness.
explanation.walkthrough: Auntie and the Beeb are both British nicknames for the BBC. 'harnessing' puts L and ZEBU, a humped ox, inside BEEB; the 's after 'Old nick' simply stands for 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are names for the Devil: the first a folksy English nickname, the second biblical, the prince of demons.

clue.text: Catch girl close to rodeo

parts.note: lass is a Scottish and northern English word for a girl

indicators.note: close is a noun here, the end of something, so take the final letter of the next word

explanation.surface: Grab hold of a girl who is standing near the rodeo.
explanation.walkthrough: 'close to' looks like 'near', but close is a noun here, the end, so it gives the last letter of rodeo. The rodeo scene is where the answer belongs.
explanation.definitionFit: As a verb it means to rope an animal with a noose, which is one way of capturing it.

clue.text: Star's in bed for a smoke

indicators.note: in places the word for a star within the word for a bed

parts.note: a cot is a small bed, for a baby in Britain or a camper in America
the star of a story or film is its hero; the 's stands for 'is' and gives no letters

explanation.surface: A celebrity is lying in bed enjoying a cigarette.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Star' is the lead of a story, a HERO, and 'in' puts it inside COT. The 's stands for 'is', and 'for' links the wordplay to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: it is a cigar cut square at both ends, and informally any cigar or cigarette is 'a smoke'.

clue.text: Calcium, lithium, fluorine or nickel, I'm thinking, make up rare metal

parts.note: Ca is the chemical symbol for calcium
Li is the chemical symbol for lithium
F is the chemical symbol for fluorine
taken as written
Ni is the chemical symbol for nickel
um is the noise a speaker makes while thinking what to say next

explanation.surface: Someone ponders which of four chemical elements go into making a scarce metal.
explanation.walkthrough: No indicator is needed: four chemical symbols, the plain word OR and UM, the noise of someone thinking, are read off in order. 'make up' joins them to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: a radioactive metallic element made only in minute quantities in reactors, so genuinely scarce.

clue.text: What baffles one listener, two of them keeping quiet

indicators.note: keeping means holding: the two words for a listener hold the letter for quiet between them

parts.note: 'them' looks back to 'listener', and an ear is what listens: this is the first of two words for one
the second word for the organ that listens: lug is British slang for it, as in lughole
P is short for piano, the musical direction to play quietly

explanation.surface: Something puzzles one member of the audience, while two others stay silent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'baffles' means deadens sound, not puzzles, so the listener is an ear, not someone in an audience. 'two of them' wants two words for that organ, the second being British slang, LUG, and 'keeping' has the pair hold the quiet letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Descriptive definition: to baffle sound is to deaden it, and this stopper deadens the noise reaching a single ear.

clue.text: The Spanish besieging a grand old African capital

indicators.note: an army besieging a town surrounds it, so the Spanish word goes around the next two pieces

parts.note: los is a Spanish word for 'the', used before masculine plural nouns
taken as written
G is short for grand, slang for a thousand pounds or dollars

explanation.surface: Spain's army lays siege to a splendid ancient city in Africa.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The Spanish' is not an army but Spanish for 'the', LOS, and 'besieging' wraps it round A and G. 'old' belongs to the definition: Abuja replaced Lagos as Nigeria's capital in 1991.
explanation.definitionFit: Factual: the city was Nigeria's seat of government until 1991, when Abuja replaced it, so 'old' means former.

clue.text: Islands, quiet in the past, engaged in festivities

indicators.note: something engaged in an activity is caught up inside it, so these pieces sit within the word for festivities

parts.note: galas are festive public celebrations
P is short for piano, the musical direction to play quietly
ago means in the past, as in 'long ago'

explanation.surface: A group of islands, once peaceful, is now busy with celebrations.
explanation.walkthrough: 'quiet in the past' looks like an insertion but is two pieces read in a row, a letter then a three-letter word, making PAGO. 'engaged in' is the real insertion, tucking that run into the festivities.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: a Pacific archipelago belonging to Ecuador, famous for the giant tortoises and finches that Darwin studied.

clue.text: We EU solvers need to get organised

indicators.note: letters that need to get organised are in a muddle and must be sorted into a different order

parts.note: taken as written: these nine letters are the muddle to sort

explanation.surface: Crossword fans across Europe admit they should sort their lives out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'need to get organised' asks you to rearrange EU SOLVERS. The definition is only the first word, 'We', taken as the emphatic pronoun.
explanation.definitionFit: Pronoun for pronoun: the emphatic first person plural, which dictionaries gloss as 'we or us in person'.

clue.text: Eg Tommy presenting diamond to Norma perhaps

parts.note: rock is slang for a diamond or other large gemstone
Norma is an opera by Bellini; 'perhaps' shows it is only one example of its kind

explanation.surface: A chap called Tommy, for example, is handing a diamond to a woman who may be called Norma.
explanation.walkthrough: Tommy is not a suitor but The Who's 1969 album, and Norma is not his girl but Bellini's opera. 'presenting' and 'to' only join the definition and the two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: Tommy is The Who's 1969 album telling the story of a deaf, dumb and blind pinball wizard in song.

clue.text: Oscar-winning UK films distributed with 100 traditional tunes

indicators.note: to win a prize is to gain it, so the rearranged letters take in the letter for Oscar
distributed means dealt out, so the letters of the two words before it are spread into a new order

parts.note: taken as written: the seven letters to be dealt out
Oscar is the word for the letter O in the NATO spelling alphabet
C is the Roman numeral for 100

explanation.surface: Award-winning British movies went out to cinemas with a hundred old songs on the soundtrack.
explanation.walkthrough: 'distributed' rearranges UK FILMS into FLKMUSI, and 'winning' lets that gain the O of Oscar (NATO alphabet), giving FOLKMUSI. 'with' adds C, the Roman numeral for 100.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by description: the songs and melodies handed down within a community over generations.

clue.text: Top conductor west gets strong, up to no good

parts.note: Mae West was the Hollywood star of the 1930s; her surname stands for her first name

indicators.note: up to means as far as: read the word strong only as far as its letters for 'no good', and stop

parts.note: taken as written, before it is cut short

explanation.surface: A leading orchestra conductor out west grows powerful and starts misbehaving.
explanation.walkthrough: 'west' is Mae West, the film star, giving MAE. 'up to' reads STRONG only as far as its NG (no good), leaving STRO, and 'gets' joins the two.
explanation.definitionFit: Honorific: Italian for master, the title given to a distinguished director of an orchestra.

clue.text: Letter from Greek ambassador stops times article

indicators.note: to stop a gap is to plug it, so the ambassador's letters plug the gap between the letters for times

parts.note: T is the abbreviation for time, so the plural, times, gives two of them
HE stands for His or Her Excellency, the formal title of an ambassador
a is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: A letter from Greece's ambassador has halted a piece in The Times newspaper.
explanation.walkthrough: The letter belongs to an alphabet, not the post. 'stops' means plugs: HE (His Excellency, an ambassador's title) fills the gap between the two Ts of 'times', and A follows.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: the eighth character of the Greek alphabet, written like an O with a bar across it.

clue.text: East end star meets mate in Paris, giving big wave

indicators.note: end points to the final letter of the word just before it, East

parts.note: the Sun is the star at the centre of our solar system
ami is the French word for a friend or mate; 'in Paris' asks for the French

explanation.surface: A soap star from London's East End greets a Parisian friend with an enormous wave.
explanation.walkthrough: London's East End is the setting of the BBC soap EastEnders, so 'East end star' suggests a soap actor. Here 'end' just takes the last letter of East, and the wave is water, not a greeting.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: a huge sea surge set off by an undersea earthquake, from the Japanese for 'harbour wave'.

clue.text: Packed theatre rented middle of field

parts.note: rep is short for repertory, a theatre whose resident company stages a rotation of plays
in British usage a flat that is let is rented out

indicators.note: middle of asks for the central letter of the five-letter word that follows

explanation.surface: A sold-out theatre company hired the centre of a meadow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Packed' looks like it describes the theatre but stands alone as the definition. REP is British shorthand for repertory theatre, LET is British for rented out, and 'middle of' takes the E of field.
explanation.definitionFit: Adjective synonyms: both mean filled to capacity, as a hall crammed with people is.

clue.text: Bird heading off hound

indicators.note: heading off tells you the head, the first letter, comes off the word for a hound

parts.note: a beagle is a small hound bred for hunting hares

explanation.surface: A bird swoops in to cut off a chasing dog.
explanation.walkthrough: 'heading off' reads as intercepting, but it tells you the head letter comes off: BEAGLE loses its B.
explanation.definitionFit: Example of the class: a large bird of prey with broad wings and a hooked beak.

clue.text: Issue eggs, round, very classy, after hours

parts.note: the letter O is round in shape
U means upper-class in British usage, from the 1950s labels 'U and non-U' for speech and manners
after hours means beyond normal closing time, which is late

explanation.surface: Someone hands out eggs, plump and very posh ones, once the shop has shut.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Issue' means emit, not hand out. There is no indicator, just four pieces in a row; U for 'classy' is the British label for upper-class speech and manners.
explanation.definitionFit: Biological sense: to release egg cells from the ovary, 'issue' meaning to send out.

clue.text: Dress boxer with coat of green

parts.note: Muhammad Ali, the heavyweight champion, is the boxer crosswords reach for first

indicators.note: a coat is an outer covering, so keep only the first and last letters of the word that follows

explanation.surface: Put a green jacket on a prizefighter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dress' is the military verb: troops dress their ranks by forming a straight line. 'coat of' takes the first and last letters of green.
explanation.definitionFit: Military sense: soldiers told to dress ranks move into a perfectly straight line.

clue.text: Block some entertaining others

indicators.note: some says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Stop certain people from amusing the rest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Block' reads as a verb meaning obstruct, but it is a noun. 'some' says the answer is a part of 'entertaining others', running across the gap between the two words.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: a bar of cast metal such as gold or steel is a solid block.

clue.text: Pineapple contains popular syrup

indicators.note: contains says the word for a pineapple holds the letters for popular inside it

parts.note: pineapple is soldiers' slang for a hand grenade, whose segmented casing looks like the fruit
whatever is popular or fashionable is 'in'

explanation.surface: The tropical fruit is full of a much-loved sweet syrup.
explanation.walkthrough: The pineapple is not the fruit: it is soldiers' slang for a hand grenade, from the segmented casing. 'contains' asks that weapon to hold a two-letter word for popular, in the sense of fashionable.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: a sweet red cordial, traditionally made from pomegranates, used to colour cocktails.

clue.text: Every so often reveal catch

indicators.note: every so often means at regular intervals: take every second letter of the next word

explanation.surface: Now and then, let people see the snag in the deal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Every so often' takes the second, fourth and sixth letters of reveal. The catch is not a snag but something an angler lands.
explanation.definitionFit: Loose example: a snakelike fish, and whatever an angler lands is called a catch.

clue.text: Reportedly fails to catch married lady's address

indicators.note: reportedly means as people say it, so the phrase that follows is heard, not spelt

parts.note: a fielder who fails to catch the ball misses it

explanation.surface: Word is that someone didn't quite hear where the married woman lives.
explanation.walkthrough: 'address' is a form of address, a title, not where she lives. 'Reportedly' signals a soundalike: say MISSES and you have pronounced the title.
explanation.definitionFit: Crossword sense of address as a form of address: the title placed before a wife's surname.

clue.text: Running is not compulsory, taking in a long period

indicators.note: taking in means absorbing, so the word for not compulsory swallows the word for a long period

parts.note: something that is not compulsory is optional
an era is a long stretch of history

explanation.surface: Nobody has to go jogging, which eats up a great deal of time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Running' is not the sport but an adjective, as in 'up and running'. 'taking in' has the word for 'not compulsory' absorb a three-letter long period, and 'is' only joins the two halves of the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Adjective synonyms: a machine that is working and in service is said to be up and running.
